doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Mr. Griffin, the boss of the street, and the soul food shooting
summary: While working with Cookie, Mr. Griffin got him home safely and pulled him under a table when a man returned with a rifle at a restaurant.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Oh because I see so many guys that their parents were just like totally against it, this is a bad idea, and I thought boy. But I mean I started playing professionally when I was 14. But it was always with relatives. I had to get home. Even when I worked with Cookie, we had what we used to call the Boss of the Street, Mr. Griffin, who was like in the black mafia or something, you know numbers, writers and all this kind of stuff. And he made sure I got home every night, every night. It was funny. I remember one time — and on the weekends he would let me stop at the soul food restaurant. I said, “Mr. Griffin can we stop?” I remember one night we stopped at this soul food restaurant on Worthington Street and we’re sitting there eating, and Mr. Griffin was this great big, he was like six two, a big, big rough guy. And we’re sitting there in the restaurant and some guy comes in and he ordered his food and then there’s a big fight. And I’ll be back mother fucker, and all this stuff like that. The guy goes, and we’re getting ready to leave ourselves, he goes and he comes back with a rifle. And you should have seen — even Mr. Griffin — Mr. Griffin grabs me and he pulls me down under the table and everything. And these guys are, you know just arguing and you don’t know if this guy’s going to shoot the guy or not. And somebody snuck up in back of the guy and grabbed the rifle. And then we just got out of there. But it was so fast. And Mr. Griffin, he was under the table before I was.
He knows how to take care of himself I guess.
